hints: Think about which two functional groups react when a dicarboxylic acid meets a diol, and what small molecule is lost each time a new link forms.
Focus on showing only one acid plus one diol joined together, with the new $\text{C-O}$ ester bond drawn out in full with the $\text{C=O}$ visible.
walkthrough:
Spot the polyester pair**
You have maleic acid, $\text{HOOC-CH=CH-COOH}$, a diacid, plus ethane-1,2-diol, $\text{HO-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-OH}$, a diol. When $\text{COOH}$ meets $\text{OH}$ you always get an ester, $\text{COO}$, plus water. This is condensation polymerisation.

Build just one repeat unit**
Join one acid to one diol and remove one $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ per ester link. A neat way to write it is $\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-O-CO-CH=CH-CO-}$. Keep the $\text{C=C}$ from maleic acid unchanged in the middle, and put free valency lines at the two ends to show the chain continues.

Display the new functional group**
The question insists the new group is fully displayed. That means do not write $\text{COO}$ as shorthand. Draw $\text{C}$ double bonded to $\text{O}$ and single bonded to $\text{O}$, like $\text{-C(=O)-O-}$. One displayed ester in the middle is enough to earn the mark, provided the rest contains only one of each monomer.

Final answer: One repeat unit: $\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-O-C(=O)-CH=CH-C(=O)-}$ with continuation bonds at each end.
The ester group $\text{-C(=O)-O-}$ must be fully displayed between the two monomer residues, showing $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-O}$ explicitly.

hints: Look at what changes from maleic acid to tartaric acid in Fig. 6.1, the $\text{C=C}$ becomes two $\text{C-OH}$ groups with no C-C bond cleavage.
walkthrough:
Recognise gentle addition across the double bond**
Maleic acid has $\text{-CH=CH-}$ and tartaric acid has $\text{-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-}$. You are adding two $\text{OH}$ groups across the $\text{C=C}$ without breaking the carbon skeleton. That is mild oxidation, not hot concentrated oxidation which would cleave the chain.
The classic reagent is cold dilute acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$, which decolourises as the diol forms.
Final answer: Cold, dilute, acidified $\text{KMnO}_{4}\text{(aq)}$ / $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$.

hints: In step 1 the two $\text{-OH}$ groups of tartaric acid react with $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{3}$ to give the cyclic $\text{O-C(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{-O}$ bridge in T, think about what small molecule must be lost.
walkthrough:
See water leaving to make the ring**
Two alcohol $\text{OH}$ groups attack the ketone $\text{C=O}$ of propanone under acid to form a cyclic ketal plus $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Whenever two molecules join with loss of water it is classified as condensation, also acceptable as dehydration or elimination.
Final answer: Condensation (dehydration / elimination).

hints: Start from what any ligand must have available to bond to a metal, think about lone pairs.
Now add what makes it bidentate rather than monodentate, think about how many such bonds one ligand forms to the same central ion.
walkthrough:
Recall what a ligand does**
A ligand is an electron pair donor. Picture an oxygen atom in $\text{-COO}^{-}$ with lone pairs reaching out to $\text{Cu}^{2+}$. The bond formed is dative covalent, meaning both shared electrons come from the ligand.

Add the meaning of bi-dentate**
Bi means two. Ligand U has two $\text{-COO}^{-}$ groups, so one U ion can donate two pairs to the same copper ion, forming two coordinate bonds and a chelate ring. That two point attachment is bidentate.
Final answer: A species with two lone pairs of electrons that each form a dative / coordinate bond to the same central transition metal atom / ion.

hints: Visualise $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ octahedrally surrounded by three $\text{O-O}$ chelates, each chelate spans adjacent positions, not opposite positions.
Think of the propeller analogy for $\text{[Cu(oxalate)}_{3}\text{]}^{4-}$, the two optical isomers are left handed and right handed propellers that are mirror images.
walkthrough:
Place three chelates octahedrally**
Draw $\text{Cu}$ with one vertical bond line as a guide. Each U is an $\text{O-O}$ arc. In an octahedron each bidentate must occupy two adjacent octahedral sites, at about 90 degrees, never trans across the metal. Arrange three such arcs around $\text{Cu}$ to complete six $\text{Cu-O}$ bonds.

Create the pair of mirror images**
Now imagine looking down the threefold axis. The three arcs look like a three bladed propeller. Draw one version twisting clockwise and the second version twisting anticlockwise. They must be mirror images that cannot be superimposed, which is why $\text{[Cu(U)}_{3}\text{]}^{4-}$ shows optical isomerism with no plane of symmetry.

Final answer: Two octahedral 3D diagrams with $\text{Cu}$ in centre and three $\text{O-O}$ bidentate arcs occupying cis positions.
One diagram shows the $\Delta$ propeller arrangement and the other shows the mirror image $\Lambda$ arrangement, non-superimposable.

hints: Count the distinct vertical lines in the carbon-13 spectrum in Fig. 6.4, each line corresponds to one different carbon environment.
walkthrough:
Count peaks, not ppm**
In $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR each different carbon environment gives one signal. Counting the lines in Fig. 6.4 gives eight separate resonances, so X has eight different carbon environments. Since the formula is $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{3}$, every carbon is in a unique environment.
Final answer: 8 / eight

hints: Remember which protons disappear when $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$ is added, think about $\text{O-H}$ protons that can rapidly swap with deuterium.
walkthrough:
Use D2O to hide exchangeable H**
Protons on $\text{O}$ such as phenolic $\text{OH}$ are acidic and labile. They exchange rapidly: $\text{R-OH + D}_{2}\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{R-OD + HOD}$. Deuterium does not appear in the $^{1}\text{H}$ spectrum, so those signals vanish. Comparing spectra with and without $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$ tells you how many $\text{OH}$ groups are present.
Final answer: To remove peaks / signals due to acidic / labile protons in $\text{OH}$ / $\text{COOH}$ by $\text{H/D}$ exchange.

hints: Use the molecular formula $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{3}$ plus aromatic plus eight $^{13}\text{C}$ signals to deduce the substitution pattern on the benzene ring.
Interpret the yellow precipitate with alkaline $\text{I}_{2}\text{(aq)}$, recall which group gives $\text{CHI}_{3}$.
Compare the number of $^{1}\text{H}$ signals in $\text{CDCl}_{3}$ (6) and $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$ (4) to find how many exchangeable $\text{OH}$ protons are present.
Match the $^{13}\text{C}$ shifts at about $\delta$ 205 and $\delta$ 60 to Table 6.2 to confirm the carbonyl type and the carbon next to it.
walkthrough:
Assemble the clues like a detective**
Formula $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{3}$ is aromatic, so $\text{C}_{6}$ ring plus $\text{C}_{2}$ side chain. Eight $^{13}\text{C}$ peaks means zero symmetry, every carbon is unique. That points to a tri-substituted benzene with three different substituents in unsymmetrical positions.

Decode the iodoform test**
Yellow precipitate with alkaline $\text{I}_{2}\text{(aq)}$ is $\text{CHI}_{3}$, the iodoform reaction: $$\text{R-CO-CH}_{3} + 3\text{I}_{2} + 4\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{R-COO}^{-}\text{Na}^{+} + \text{CHI}_{3} + 3\text{NaI} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ So X must contain a methyl ketone, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$. That accounts for $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{3}\text{O}_{1}$, leaving $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}_{2}$ for the ring plus oxygens.

Count the exchangeable protons**
$^{1}\text{H}$ NMR shows 6 signals in $\text{CDCl}_{3}$ but only 4 in $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$. The 2 lost signals are labile $\text{OH}$ protons exchanged to $\text{OD}$. So there are two $\text{OH}$ groups. Check: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-C}_{6}\text{H}_{3}\text{(OH)}_{2}$ gives $^{1}\text{H}$ environments: $\text{CH}_{3}$ (1) + 3 different aromatic H (3) + 2 different OH (2) = 6 total, falling to 4 after $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$. Perfect match.

Confirm with carbon shifts**
Table 6.2 clinches it. The $^{13}\text{C}$ peak at $\delta$ about 203 ppm lies in 190-220 ppm, characteristic of a ketone / aldehyde carbonyl, $\text{R-CO-R}$. Here it is the $\text{CH}_{3}\underline{\text{C}}\text{O}$ carbon. The peak at $\delta$ about 62 ppm lies in 30-65 ppm for carbon next to carbonyl / carboxyl, the $\text{CH}_{3}$ carbon next to $\text{C=O}$. The cluster at 110-160 ppm are the six different arene carbons. Any non-symmetrical dihydroxyacetophenone isomer fits all data.

Final answer: X is a dihydroxyphenyl methyl ketone, e.g. $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-C}_{6}\text{H}_{3}\text{(OH)}_{2}$ such as 2,4-dihydroxyacetophenone, non-symmetrical so all 8 carbons are different.
Contains $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO-}$ group because yellow $\text{CHI}_{3}$ ppt with alkaline $\text{I}_{2}\text{(aq)}$.
Contains two $\text{-OH}$ groups because $6-4 = 2$ $^{1}\text{H}$ signals lost on $\text{D}_{2}\text{O}$ shake.
Contains ketone $\text{C=O}$ because $^{13}\text{C}$ signal at $\delta$ 203 / 190-220 ppm and methyl / C next to $\text{C=O}$ because signal at $\delta$ 62 / 30-65 ppm.
